blocks.text: A newly transplanted kidney, pink and firm when the surgeon connects the vessels, turns mottled and blue within minutes as the clamps are released. The recipient already carried antibodies against the donor, and the graft is destroyed before the operation is finished. Matching, in transplantation, is about preventing exactly this.

blocks.markdown: A **transplant** from a genetically different person is recognised as foreign because the recipient's T cells and antibodies detect **alloantigens**, mainly donor **HLA** (MHC) molecules, which are highly polymorphic. T cells can see donor HLA by **direct allorecognition** (recipient T cells recognising intact donor HLA on donor antigen-presenting cells, accounting for a very large fraction of responding T cells early on) and **indirect allorecognition** (recipient APCs processing donor HLA and presenting peptides on recipient MHC, important in the longer term).

rows: Pre-formed antibodies (anti-ABO, or anti-HLA from previous pregnancy, transfusion or transplant) bind donor endothelium, activating complement (type II) and causing thrombosis
Immediate graft loss; not treatable; prevented by ABO matching and crossmatching
Days to weeks (commonest in the first months)
T cell-mediated (CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ recognising donor HLA) and/or antibody-mediated; interstitial infiltrate, tubulitis in kidney
Ongoing immune injury (indirect recognition, antibody) plus non-immune factors, causing vascular intimal thickening and fibrosis
Slow progressive loss of function; poorly responsive to treatment
blocks.caption: Types of rejection by timing and mechanism

blocks.title: Which type of rejection?
blocks.prompt: A patient receives a kidney transplant. Nine days later she has fever, graft tenderness and a rising creatinine. Biopsy shows lymphocytes infiltrating the tubules. Previous crossmatch was negative. Classify the rejection and explain.

steps.text: Timing: nine days after transplant fits acute rejection (days to weeks), not hyperacute (minutes to hours) or chronic (months to years).
Mechanism: a negative crossmatch excludes significant pre-formed donor-specific antibody, and the biopsy shows lymphocytes invading tubules (tubulitis), indicating T cell-mediated attack.
Conclude: acute cellular rejection, in which recipient T cells recognise donor HLA directly.
Management principle: acute cellular rejection often responds to intensified immunosuppression, because the T cell response can still be suppressed.

blocks.answer: Acute T cell-mediated rejection; usually reversible with treatment.

blocks.markdown: **ABO and HLA matching.** **ABO** antigens are expressed on red cells and endothelium. Individuals have natural IgM antibodies to the ABO antigens they lack (group O has anti-A and anti-B; group A has anti-B; group B has anti-A; group AB has neither). ABO-incompatible organs are rapidly rejected by pre-formed antibody, so ABO compatibility is required for most organ transplants. Group O red cells can be given to any recipient and AB recipients can receive any group.

**HLA matching.** The HLA loci most important to outcome are **HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR** (class I and class II). The better the match, the fewer foreign peptides the recipient sees, and the lower the risk of rejection and need for immunosuppression. HLA genes are inherited as a block called a **haplotype** from each parent. A full match between siblings means sharing both haplotypes. Before transplantation, a **crossmatch** mixes recipient serum with donor lymphocytes to detect pre-formed donor-specific antibody; a positive crossmatch generally contraindicates the transplant. Sensitisation to HLA (pregnancy, transfusion, prior transplant) is measured as **panel-reactive antibody (PRA)**, the percentage of a panel of donors against whom the recipient has antibodies.

blocks.latex: P(\text{full sibling match}) = \dfrac{1}{4},\qquad P(\text{at least one match among } n) = 1 - \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{n}
blocks.caption: Each sibling inherits one of two haplotypes from each parent; four combinations are equally likely

blocks.title: Finding a sibling donor
blocks.prompt: A patient needing a transplant has three full siblings. Assuming haplotypes segregate independently of one another (no recombination), what is the probability that at least one is a full HLA match?

steps.text: Each sibling has a 1 in 4 chance of sharing both haplotypes, so a 3 in 4 chance of not matching.
For three siblings, all must fail to match.
Interpret: about a 58% chance. Even with several siblings, there is a substantial chance that none is a full match, which is why registries of unrelated donors are used.

blocks.markdown: **Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).** GVHD complicates **haematopoietic stem cell transplantation** (HSCT) and occasionally transfusion of non-irradiated blood to immunodeficient patients. It arises when three conditions hold: the graft contains **immunocompetent donor T cells**, the recipient has **HLA or minor histocompatibility antigens that the donor does not**, and the recipient is **unable to reject** the donor cells (because of conditioning chemotherapy or radiotherapy, or underlying immunodeficiency). Donor T cells recognise recipient tissue as foreign and attack it. **Acute GVHD** (usually within about 100 days) affects the skin (rash), liver (jaundice) and gut (diarrhoea). **Chronic GVHD** resembles autoimmune disease with skin sclerosis, dry eyes and mouth and organ fibrosis. The same donor T cells attack residual leukaemia (the graft-versus-leukaemia effect), a benefit that cannot easily be separated from GVHD. Mitigating measures include HLA matching, T cell depletion, and immunosuppression.

blocks.title: Recipient is attacked, not the graft
blocks.text: Rejection is host versus graft; GVHD is graft versus host. In GVHD the transplanted lymphocytes are the aggressors, so the key risk is immune cells in the graft and an unreactive recipient, not HLA mismatch alone.

blocks.title: Prevent what you can
blocks.text: Hyperacute rejection is prevented by ABO compatibility and a negative crossmatch. Acute rejection is minimised by HLA matching and immunosuppression. GVHD is reduced by matching and by controlling donor T cells.

points: Hyperacute rejection (minutes to hours) is due to pre-formed antibody; acute (days to weeks) is mainly T cell-mediated; chronic (months to years) is slow vascular and fibrotic damage.
ABO compatibility, HLA-A, -B and -DR matching and a negative crossmatch improve outcomes; PRA measures sensitisation.
GVHD occurs when donor T cells in the graft attack an immunocompromised recipient with different HLA; acute GVHD affects skin, liver and gut.

questions.stem: Which type of rejection occurs within minutes to hours of vascular anastomosis and is caused by pre-formed antibodies?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pre-formed antibody and complement cause rapid graft destruction.
distractorRationale.b: Acute cellular rejection occurs days to weeks later and is T cell-mediated.
distractorRationale.c: Chronic rejection occurs over months to years.
distractorRationale.d: GVHD is donor lymphocytes attacking the host.

questions.explanation: Hyperacute rejection is mediated by pre-existing antibodies to donor ABO or HLA antigens which bind endothelium and activate complement, causing thrombosis within minutes to hours.

questions.stem: A transplant recipient develops a slow, progressive decline in graft function eight years after transplantation, with biopsy showing vascular intimal thickening and fibrosis. Which description fits?

distractorRationale.b: Acute rejection occurs earlier and is more cellular.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: chronic rejection features vasculopathy and fibrosis over years.

questions.explanation: Chronic rejection involves progressive vascular and fibrotic damage over months or years, caused by ongoing immune injury with other factors, and responds poorly to treatment.

questions.stem: Why is ABO compatibility needed before most solid organ transplants?

options.text: Recipients have natural antibodies against ABO antigens they lack, which can cause hyperacute rejection
ABO antigens are minor and unimportant
ABO antigens are only on lymphocytes

questions.correctOptionText: Recipients have natural antibodies against ABO antigens they lack, which can cause hyperacute rejection

distractorRationale.a: Correct: natural anti-A or anti-B IgM bind graft endothelium.
distractorRationale.b: ABO antigens are expressed on endothelium and are major barriers.
distractorRationale.c: ABO antigens are on red cells and endothelium.
distractorRationale.d: GVHD is caused by donor T cells.

questions.explanation: People carry natural IgM against the ABO antigens they lack. An incompatible organ displays those antigens on its endothelium, causing complement activation and hyperacute rejection.

questions.stem: A crossmatch is positive when the recipient's serum is mixed with donor lymphocytes. What does this indicate?

options.text: Donor-specific antibodies are present, so transplantation is generally contraindicated
There is no risk of rejection

questions.correctOptionText: Donor-specific antibodies are present, so transplantation is generally contraindicated

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pre-formed donor-specific antibody risks hyperacute rejection.
distractorRationale.d: The risk of rejection is high.

questions.explanation: A positive crossmatch means that the recipient has antibodies that bind donor cells, predicting hyperacute rejection, so the transplant is usually not performed.

questions.stem: Which combination is necessary for GVHD to develop?

options.text: Immunocompetent donor T cells, recipient antigens foreign to the donor and a recipient unable to reject the graft
Recipient T cells, matched HLA and a healthy immune system

questions.correctOptionText: Immunocompetent donor T cells, recipient antigens foreign to the donor and a recipient unable to reject the graft

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these are the three requirements.
distractorRationale.b: With matched HLA and a healthy immune system, GVHD is unlikely.
distractorRationale.c: Donor T cells, not just B cells, are the effectors.
distractorRationale.d: Pre-formed recipient antibody causes hyperacute rejection, not GVHD.

questions.explanation: Donor T cells recognise recipient HLA or minor antigens as foreign and, if the recipient cannot eliminate them, attack skin, liver and gut.

questions.stem: True or false: acute GVHD classically affects the skin, liver and gastrointestinal tract.
questions.explanation: Acute GVHD typically causes rash, cholestatic jaundice and diarrhoea, reflecting donor T cell attack on these tissues.

questions.stem: A patient has 2 full siblings. Assuming that each has a 1 in 4 chance of being a full HLA match, what is the probability, in percent, that at least one is a full match?
questions.explanation: The chance that a given sibling is not a match is 3/4. For two siblings, 3/4 × 3/4 = 0.5625. The chance at least one matches is 1 - 0.5625 = 0.4375, or 43.75%.

questions.stem: A recipient is tested against a panel of 200 donors. Her serum reacts against 150 of them. Calculate the panel-reactive antibody (PRA) as a percentage, and from this the percentage of donors to whom she is unreactive. Give the percentage unreactive.
questions.explanation: PRA = 150/200 = 75%. Donors to whom she is not reactive = 100% - 75% = 25%. A highly sensitised patient therefore has few compatible donors and waits longer.

questions.stem: Distinguish hyperacute, acute and chronic rejection by timing and mechanism.
markingGuide: Hyperacute: minutes to hours; pre-formed antibodies and complement; thrombosis
Acute: days to weeks; T cell-mediated (and antibody); infiltrate; often reversible
Chronic: months to years; vascular intimal thickening and fibrosis; progressive; poor response to treatment
questions.explanation: Timing correlates with mechanism: pre-formed antibody acts immediately, primed T cells over days to weeks, and chronic vascular injury over years.

questions.stem: Explain how GVHD arises after bone marrow transplantation and why ABO and HLA matching matter in transplantation generally.
markingGuide: GVHD requires immunocompetent donor T cells, recipient antigens foreign to donor and recipient unable to reject
Donor T cells attack skin, liver, gut
HLA matching reduces foreign peptide presentation and reduces rejection and GVHD
ABO matching avoids pre-formed anti-ABO antibodies causing hyperacute rejection
HLA-A, B, DR most important; crossmatch detects donor-specific antibody
questions.explanation: Matching reduces both host-versus-graft and graft-versus-host responses.
